title: A Patronus in the Corridor
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 13 of 40
content:
The Dementor should not have been inside Hogwarts.

That was the first problem.

The second was that it found us underground.

I was carrying a tray of sealed samples from the dungeon to a temporary testing room on the second floor. Snape walked beside me with the evidence ledger tucked under one arm. We had just reached the corridor beneath the marble staircase when every torch went blue.

The air changed.

Cold did not arrive from outside. It opened inside my chest.

My next breath hurt.

Snape stopped so abruptly I nearly struck him with the tray.

“What—”

“Quiet.”

His wand was already out.

At the far end of the corridor, darkness moved.

Not shadow.

Fabric.

Rotting hands.

A hood where a face should have been.

My mind knew the word before my body accepted it.

Dementor.

I had seen one once from a distance.

Distance had lied.

Up close, the creature did not merely frighten. It emptied. The corridor vanished beneath memories I had not invited: rooms I had left, voices I did not want, every private failure suddenly arranged as proof that hope had always been vanity.

The tray slipped in my hands.

Snape caught it.

“Look at me.”

I could not.

The Dementor glided closer.

A scream echoed somewhere.

Mine? Someone else's? Memory did not care.

“Look at me.”

Snape's voice cut through the cold.

I forced my eyes toward him.

His face was pale, jaw clenched so hard I could see the muscle jump.

He was afraid too.

That helped.

Not because I wanted him frightened.

Because he was not standing outside the terror instructing me how to survive it. He was in it.

“Patronus,” I managed.

“Yes.”

My wand shook.

I tried.

Nothing happened.

The cold deepened.

Snape turned toward the Dementor.

For one second, his face cracked.

I saw grief.

Then his wand moved.

Silver light exploded through the corridor.

A doe landed between us and the Dementor.

Beautiful was the wrong word.

It was too alive for that.

The Patronus bounded forward, light spilling from its body across the stones. The Dementor recoiled. The doe drove it backward, step by impossible step, until it vanished around the corner.

Warmth returned slowly.

The Patronus remained.

It turned.

Its silver head lifted toward Snape.

He looked at it as though no one else existed.

I knew what it meant.

Everyone did by then.

Harry Potter's testimony had been repeated in every paper that printed Snape's name. Lily Evans Potter. The doe. A love carried across decades.

The story had become public property.

Standing there, I hated that for him.

The Patronus approached.

Snape held out his hand.

Its nose touched his fingers without touching them.

Light trembled across his face.

Then he lowered his wand.

The doe vanished.

Silence remained.

I looked away first.

Snape's voice came cold and controlled.

“Are you injured?”

“No.”

“Can you walk?”

“Yes.”

“Then take the samples to McGonagall. Tell her a Dementor breached the west corridor.”

“What about you?”

“I shall find out how.”

“Alone?”

His eyes snapped toward me.

“Do not.”

“I asked a practical question.”

“No. You are about to offer sympathy.”

“I wasn't.”

“Your face says otherwise.”

“My face is recovering from a Dementor.”

His expression hardened.

I understood suddenly.

He did not want to stand there while I looked at him and thought Lily.

Not because Lily did not matter.

Because for years, perhaps decades, she had been the only explanation anyone bothered to attach to his better actions. The doe had become a verdict: proof that he could love, proof that he had changed, proof that he had never moved on, proof of whatever anyone wanted his life to mean.

I shifted the tray to one arm.

“That was exceptional casting,” I said.

He blinked.

“The Patronus,” I continued. “Full corporeal form under immediate exposure. Fast response. Strong enough to drive it around a corner.”

His brow furrowed.

“You are evaluating my technique.”

“Yes.”

“Now.”

“You taught me to notice competence.”

For one astonishing second, he looked offended and relieved at the same time.

“The casting angle was inefficient,” he said.

“Of course it was.”

“The corridor narrowed the approach.”

“Tragic.”

His mouth twitched.

There.

Not fixed.

Not safe.

But back in the present.

We found the breach together.

A Ministry transport team had brought two Dementors to the grounds that morning as part of a prisoner transfer from an old holding site near Hogsmeade. One had slipped its restraints during a storm-charm failure.

McGonagall's response to this explanation could have peeled paint.

By sunset, the Ministry had removed both creatures and sent four separate apologies.

Snape found this inadequate.

I agreed.

That evening, I returned to the dungeon to collect my case.

He was there alone.

The classroom lamps were low.

His back was to me.

“You left the evidence ledger upstairs,” I said.

“I know.”

I set it on the table.

He did not turn.

I should have left.

Instead I asked, “Are you all right?”

“No.”

The answer stopped me.

He turned then.

His face looked exhausted.

“I am not,” he repeated. “The creature was in the castle. Again.”

Again.

I remembered the years when Dementors had guarded Hogwarts.

“How bad was it for you?”

His laugh held no humor.

“You ask remarkably broad questions.”

“You can give a narrow answer.”

He looked at the empty classroom.

“I heard her.”

I did not ask who.

“Lily?”

He flinched at the name, but nodded.

“What did you hear?”

“No.”

“Okay.”

His eyes lifted, wary.

I leaned against a table.

“You don't have to make the memory useful to me.”

Something in his face loosened.

We stood quietly.

After a while, he said, “I also heard Albus.”

I waited.

“And?”

“And myself.”

That seemed worst of all.

He sat.

I sat across from him.

“The Patronus helped me,” I said.

His expression shuttered.

“I know what it represents. I'm not asking you to explain it.”

“Then why mention it?”

“Because it helped me.”

He looked at me.

“I was stuck,” I continued. “You told me to look at you. Then you cast. Whatever memory powered it, whatever history shaped it, the thing it did in that corridor was protect both of us.”

His gaze dropped to his hands.

“That is a dangerously simple interpretation.”

“It's not an interpretation. It's what happened.”

He said nothing.

I stood.

At the door, he spoke.

“Your first attempt was poor.”

I turned.

“My Patronus?”

“Your concentration collapsed before the incantation.”

“I was being attacked by despair in a cloak.”

“Dementors are notoriously inconsiderate.”

I smiled.

“Will you teach me?”

The question left my mouth before I could examine it.

Snape went still.

“Potter had Lupin,” he said.

“I have you.”

Silence.

The words sounded more intimate than I intended.

Neither of us looked away.

At last he said, “Tomorrow. After the audit.”

My pulse jumped.

“Thank you.”

“Do not thank me until you manage a corporeal form.”

“I may thank you out of spite.”

“That would be consistent.”

I left before my face could betray too much.

Behind me, the dungeon door closed softly.

I had seen the doe.

What stayed with me was not jealousy.

It was the way Snape had looked at me through the cold and told me to stay present.

The next afternoon, our first Patronus lesson was a disaster.

Mine, specifically.

“Again,” Snape said.

A thin spray of silver mist coughed from my wand and immediately vanished.

“I am doing it.”

“You are performing the motion while anticipating failure. Those are not equivalent.”

“Helpful.”

“I was not attempting to be comforting.”

“I noticed.”

He circled behind me without touching, correcting the angle of my wand with words alone. His voice was still rough from the injury, but teaching changed it. The rasp became less fragile when wrapped around precision.

“Do not select the grandest happy memory you possess merely because it sounds impressive,” he said. “Use one you trust.”

“What did you use?”

He went still.

I regretted the question immediately.

“You don't have to answer.”

“No.” His eyes stayed on my wand. “I do not.”

There was no anger in it.

That itself felt like progress.

I tried again with something smaller: warm food after a long day, clean sheets, a laugh I had not expected.

The mist lasted two seconds longer.

Snape inclined his head.

“Better.”

For some reason, that one word felt better than applause.

Tomorrow, he was going to teach me how to do the same for myself.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
